Plan of the class

This module is read in one hour. It continues Topic 5 where Class 15 stopped: you can now recognize an anomaly (lesson 5.1) and put alerts in order of urgency (lesson 5.2). Today you take one alert to the end of the process: you analyze it, you diagnose it, you document the result and you tell the right people.

5.3

Analyze

Five steps: collect, timeline, benign explanations first, corroborate, conclude.

5.4

Diagnose and document

Category, root cause, scope, exposure window, impact, priority, confidence; evidence integrity; the diagnosis record.

5.5

Communicate

Who needs to know, when, through which channel, under which label; plain language; the law of Québec and Canada.

Quiz

Quiz 3 (5%)

Topics 3 and 4 as taught (lessons 3.1 to 3.5, 4.1 and 4.2). What it covers and how to prepare are at the end of this module.

Slide 4

Learning outcomes

By the end of this class, you will be able to:

  1. Analyze an alert with five steps (collect, timeline, benign explanations first, corroborate, conclude) and produce a timeline and a hypothesis table lesson 5.3.
  2. Diagnose the result: category (security incident, monitoring failure or benign), root cause, scope, exposure window, impact on confidentiality, integrity and availability, priority, ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge) technique when there is an attacker, and confidence lesson 5.4.
  3. Protect the integrity of evidence with SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit) hashes, an evidence register and a chain of custody, and write a diagnosis record that separates facts from interpretations lesson 5.4.
  4. Communicate the result: decide who must be informed, when, through which channel and under which TLP (Traffic Light Protocol) label; check the notification duties of Québec and Canadian law; write a plain-language note for the owner and a technical annex for the people who fix the problem lesson 5.5.

Competency EZ01 (Monitor a computer network from a cybersecurity perspective), element 4, Detection and diagnosis of anomalies: methodical analysis of network traffic, network files and event logs; rigorous analysis of anomalies; accurate diagnosis of incidents. Today's class also works on five performance criteria that apply to the whole competency: effective communication with stakeholders, considering various sources of information, accurate interpretation of available data, respect for the confidentiality of the monitoring data collected, and effective priority management.

In Class 15 you sorted the twelve alerts of the weekend of October 9 to 10. Triage decided the order of work; it did not decide what happened. A P1 (priority 1) alert can turn out to be a backup job, and a P3 (priority 3) alert can turn out to be a real weakness. Only the analysis can show which.

The three lessons of today correspond to two categories of the Respond function of the NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) Cybersecurity Framework 2.0: Incident Analysis (RS.AN (Respond function, Incident Analysis category), lessons 5.3 and 5.4) and Incident Response Reporting and Communication (RS.CO (Respond function, Incident Response Reporting and Communication category), lesson 5.5). The current NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) guide on incident response, NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-61 Revision 3 (April 2025), is written as a profile of that framework.

5.3

Analyzing anomalies step by step

Slide 8

Triage answered one question: which alert first? Analysis answers three others: what exactly happened, in what order, and how sure are we? The answer must come from evidence, and it must be reproducible: another technician who receives the same files and applies the same steps must reach the same conclusion.

Slide 9

5.3.1 Key terms

Analysis
The systematic examination of the records related to an alert in order to establish the facts, their order and their cause. In the NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, it is the category Incident Analysis (RS.AN): "investigations are conducted to ensure effective response and support forensics and recovery activities".
Evidence
Any record that can support or contradict a statement about what happened: an event-log entry, a console export, the state of a configuration, a change ticket, a written statement of a person.
Hypothesis
A possible explanation of the facts that makes predictions you can check: "if this explanation is true, we should find this record, and we should not find that one".
Corroboration
The confirmation of a fact by a second source that is independent of the first.
Finding
A statement that the analysis has established, written together with the evidence that supports it.
Confidence
How strongly the evidence supports a finding: low, medium or high (the criteria are in lesson 5.4).
Slide 10

5.3.2 Three errors that the method prevents

Confirmation bias

Confirmation bias is the tendency to look only for the evidence that supports the explanation you already prefer. "The antivirus stopped updating, so it must be malware", and from then on you read only the records that fit. Prevention: write every hypothesis before you read the evidence in detail, and test the benign ones first.

Mixed time zones

The antivirus console writes its times in UTC (Coordinated Universal Time), the workstations write local time with its offset, and the alert queue writes local time without any offset. Sorted without conversion, the policy change written "21:42" by the console appears after the first failure at "21:15", and the cause seems to come after its effect. Prevention: convert every time to one zone before sorting.

Single source

One record from one system shows only what that system recorded. A console can display a wrong status, a log can be incomplete, an account can be used by someone else. Prevention: confirm each important fact with at least two independent sources.

Slide 11

The steps are done in this order, and each one produces a file. These files are your working papers: they allow someone else to check your work, and they become the annexes of the diagnosis record (lesson 5.4).

Slide 12

Step 1 — Collect

  • Scope of collection. Start from the alert: the assets (WS-10-22, WS-10-37, WS-10-51), the accounts and the addresses it names (none for A-09), and a time window that begins before the first symptom and ends at the moment of collection. For A-09, the workstation logs and the update history start on Thursday, October 8, the day of the last successful update; the console audit log and the change log were exported from October 1, to check earlier changes such as Patch Wednesday (October 7).
  • Read-only methods. A read-only method copies or displays data without changing the system: an export from the console, Get-WinEvent on an event log, Get-SmbShare and Test-Path on a server. Restarting a workstation, deleting a file or "trying a fix" before collecting changes the evidence, and some of it is then lost.
  • Collection log. Each file is written in a collection log: evidence identifier, file name, source system, independence group, who collected it, when, with which method, and for which phase (analysis or verification).
  • Hash at collection. The SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit) hash of each file is computed as soon as the file is collected; lesson 5.4 explains how it proves that the file has not changed since.
  • A-09: eight files collected between 09:02 and 09:23 on Tuesday (E-01 to E-08), from five groups: console, workstations, srv-ad01, change-log and calendar.
Slide 13

The order of volatility

Some evidence disappears faster than other evidence. The order of volatility is the order in which data are lost when time passes or when a system is switched off. RFC (Request for Comments) 3227, Guidelines for Evidence Collection and Archiving (IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force), 2002), section 2.1, asks you to collect the most volatile data first:

Table 5.3-2 - Order of volatility (IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) RFC (Request for Comments) 3227, section 2.1) at a small company
OrderRFC (Request for Comments) 3227 categoryExample at Atelier NordikWhy it disappears
1Registers, cacheProcessor cache of WS-10-22 (specialist tools only)Changes millions of times per second
2Routing table, ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) cache, process table, kernel statistics, memoryGet-Process, Get-NetTCPConnection, arp -a; a memory imageLost at shutdown or after minutes of activity
3Temporary file systems%TEMP% on Windows, /tmp on srv-web01Cleaned at restart or by maintenance jobs
4DiskEvent log files, configuration files, user filesOverwritten when the log is full; modified by normal use
5Remote logging and monitoring data relevant to the systemMON-250 central logs; antivirus console exportsRemoved by retention rules (days or weeks)
6Physical configuration, network topologyLab 1 network diagram, switch and firewall configurationChanges with each project; old versions are not kept
7Archival mediaBackups of SRV-AD01Kept the longest; least volatile
Order of volatility of RFC (Request for Comments) 3227, section 2.1: collect the evidence that disappears first before the evidence that lasts.

For A-09, nothing volatile was needed: the facts were in event logs, console exports and a ticket. When an attack is still in progress, the network connections and the running processes come first, because they disappear when the program stops or the computer restarts.

Slide 14

Step 2 — Timeline in one time zone

  • A timeline is the list of all the relevant records, sorted by time and expressed in a single time zone.
  • UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) is the international reference time. Montréal uses EDT (Eastern Daylight Time) from the second Sunday of March to the first Sunday of November (in 2026, until November 1), then EST (Eastern Standard Time). In October: EDT (Eastern Daylight Time) = UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) − 4 hours.
  • Times are written in the international format ISO (International Organization for Standardization) 8601: 2026-10-08T17:42:10-04:00 is the date, the letter T, the time, then the offset from UTC (Coordinated Universal Time). A final Z means an offset of zero, in other words UTC (Coordinated Universal Time). The console's 2026-10-08T21:42:10Z is therefore Thursday, October 8, 17:42:10 EDT (Eastern Daylight Time).
  • Each row of the timeline contains: the time (one zone), the evidence identifier, the file, the line number, the record verbatim (copied exactly, never rewritten), and an interpretation of one sentence, kept separate from the record.
  • Identical records that repeat are grouped: keep the first, the last and the count. The 84 failed updates of A-09 (28 per workstation, one every 4 hours) become six rows, the first and the last failure of each workstation, with the count.
  • Check the clocks. Records from several systems can be put in order only if their clocks agree. Computers synchronize their clocks with NTP (Network Time Protocol); a drift of a few seconds matters when two events are close in time (Class 15, alert A-07: 2.4 seconds of drift on WS-10-31).
Slide 15

The A-09 timeline

Read the figure from left to right. Thursday 17:15: last successful update on each workstation (event 2000). 17:30: ticket CH-2026-090 is opened. 17:42: the console's audit log records the change of the policy Render-WS; its update source becomes the shared folder \\SRV-AD01\AVDefs, with no fallback. 17:47 to 17:51: the policy reaches the three workstations. 21:15: first failed update (event 2001), error 0x80070035, "The network path was not found." Then one failure every 4 hours on each workstation, until Tuesday 09:18. Saturday 09:30: the daily check raises A-09, 36 hours after the first failure. Tuesday 09:20: the share does not exist on SRV-AD01.

Two facts are visible only because the records are in one time zone: the change comes before the first failure (3 hours 33 minutes), and the gap between the last success (17:15) and the first failure (21:15) is exactly the 4-hour update interval. The error code is documented by Microsoft: 0x80070035 carries the Windows error 53, ERROR_BAD_NETPATH, and the events 2000 and 2001 are described in the Microsoft Defender Antivirus event reference.

Slide 16

Step 3 — Benign explanations first, then the adversary hypothesis

  • List the hypotheses before testing them. For each one, write its prediction ("if it is true, we will find…") and the test that could prove it wrong.
  • Test the benign hypotheses first, for two reasons. They are more frequent: most alerts have an ordinary cause (lesson 5.1, base rate). They are cheap to check: a maintenance calendar, a change ticket, an allow-list, a logbook, the status page of a provider.
  • Then always test the adversary hypothesis, even when a benign explanation looks sufficient. An attacker can act during a maintenance window, or make a malicious change at the same time as an approved change.
  • Each test has one of four results: supported (the predictions are found), refuted (a record contradicts a prediction), not supported (the evidence found does not support it, but cannot exclude it) or undetermined (the records needed for the test could not be obtained).
  • A refuted hypothesis is a result. Write it down: it tells the next person what has already been checked.
Slide 16

The four hypotheses of A-09

  • H1, the workstations were off or disconnected: refuted. The console saw them online on Tuesday at 09:02 (E-02), and each one tried to update every 4 hours (E-05).
  • H2, the update service of the publisher was unavailable: refuted. The nine other workstations made 102 successful updates from October 9 to 13 (E-03).
  • H3, a documented change explains the failures: supported. The ticket shows that step 2 was done and step 1 was not (E-07); the audit log shows the change at 17:42 (E-04); the workstations fail on that exact path (E-05); the share does not exist (E-06).
  • H4, an adversary tampered with the antivirus (ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge) T1685 Disable or Modify Tools): not supported. The change came from the contractor's usual account, from its usual address, after a sign-in with multi-factor authentication, under an approved ticket, and real-time protection stayed on. Because the console account itself could have been used by someone else, the analysis does not stop here: the change must be confirmed out of band, by phone (step 4).

Slide 17

Step 4 — Corroborate with independent sources

  • Two sources are independent when an error, a failure or a falsification in one of them cannot change the other: different systems, different collection paths, different administrators.
  • Two records of the same system count once. The device status (E-02), the update history (E-03) and the audit log (E-04) form one group: they come from the same console, so one fault in the console, or one stolen console account, affects all three at the same time.
  • A person contacted out of band, through a channel that is not part of the systems under investigation, is a separate source. The contact number comes from the service contract, never from an e-mail or from the console.
  • Minimum: two independent groups for a finding; three or more for high confidence.
  • A-09: H3 is supported by four groups: workstations (E-05), console (E-04), SRV-AD01 (E-06) and change log (E-07). The phone call of 09:50 adds a fifth source: the contractor confirms the change and says that step 1 was forgotten.

Two records from the same system are never independent: one fault in the console, or one stolen console account, affects every record that the console produces.
Slide 18

Step 5 — Conclude

  • Write the preliminary conclusion: the category, the ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge) technique if there is an attacker, the confidence and the open questions. Lesson 5.4 turns it into the diagnosis record.
  • Use exact words. "No evidence of X" is not "X did not happen." The absence of a record proves nothing if the source could not have recorded the event: logging not enabled, retention too short, source not collected. Write what was checked.
  • A-09, preliminary conclusion: monitoring failure; no ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge) technique (T1685 not supported, to be confirmed by phone); confidence high; exposure so far from Thursday 21:15 to Tuesday 09:18 (4 days 12 hours); priority P3 (priority 3) raised to P2 (priority 2); three open questions: confirm the change with the contractor by phone, run a full scan once the definitions are updated, and find why step 1 was skipped and why the change was not in the maintenance calendar.

Example 5.3 — Analyze alert A-09 with a script

Task

Analyze alert A-09 from the evidence pack with the five steps, and produce three files: the timeline outputs/a09_timeline.csv, the hypothesis table outputs/a09_hypotheses.csv and the preliminary findings outputs/a09_findings.json.

Relation to the lecture

Each function of the script is one step of lesson 5.3: step1_collect, step2_timeline, step3_hypotheses, step4_corroborate, step5_conclude. The script converts every time to EDT (Eastern Daylight Time), quotes every record verbatim, tests the benign hypotheses before the adversary one and counts independent groups.

Future lab

Lab 3, Part C asks for the same three outputs (timeline, hypotheses, conclusion) on two P1 (priority 1) items of your queue. Reuse the structure of this script and the template templates/timeline_template.csv; your evidence and your hypotheses will be different.

Run it yourself

Python 3.10 or later, standard library only (python.org). From the folder class16_files: python3 scripts/analyze_anomaly.py (Windows: py scripts\analyze_anomaly.py). Fictional data only; never on a real system (Legal Notice, section 6.1).

Run it on your own computer, never on a real system# (Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice v2.0, sections 6.1 and 7.2).# ===================================================================================================== # Import the csv module: it reads and writes comma-separated files and handles fields in quotes.import csv# Import the json module: the findings are saved as JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) for lesson 5.4.import json# Import the regular-expression module: it finds the collection time written in a text transcript.import re# Import date and time tools: every record must be converted to one time zone before it is sorted.from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone# Import Path: it builds file paths that work the same way on Windows, macOS and Linux.from pathlib import Path # Remember the folder that contains this script (the "scripts" folder of the downloads).HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent# The evidence folder is next to the scripts folder; nothing in it is ever modified by this script.EVIDENCE = HERE.parent / "a09_evidence"# The results go to a separate folder, so that the evidence and the analysis never mix.OUT = HERE.parent / "outputs"# Atelier Nordik is in Montreal: in October the local time is EDT (Eastern Daylight Time), UTC minus 4 hours.EDT = timezone(timedelta(hours=-4))# The three workstations named in alert A-09 are the assets the analysis is about.ASSETS = ["WS-10-22", "WS-10-37", "WS-10-51"] # Define a helper that turns any time text of the evidence pack into a date-time in EDT.def to_edt(text): # Remove spaces around the text so that a stray space does not break the conversion. text = text.strip() # A final "Z" means UTC (Coordinated Universal Time); Python before 3.11 needs it written "+00:00". if text.endswith("Z"): # Replace the "Z" by the explicit offset "+00:00", which every Python 3 version understands. text = text[:-1] + "+00:00" # Read the text as an ISO 8601 date-time (the international date and time format). moment = datetime.fromisoformat(text) # A time without an offset (for example "2026-10-10 09:30") was written in local time. if moment.tzinfo is None: # Attach the local time zone to it, without changing the clock time. moment = moment.replace(tzinfo=EDT) # Convert the moment to EDT, so that every record is expressed in the same time zone. return moment.astimezone(EDT) # Define a helper that formats a date-time the way the report shows it: "Thu 2026-10-08 17:42:10".def show(moment): # strftime writes the weekday, the date and the time; the result is the same on every computer. return moment.strftime("%a %Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S") # Define a helper that reads a CSV file of the evidence folder and returns its rows with line numbers.def read_rows(name): # Open the file in read-only mode; "newline=''" lets the csv module handle line endings itself. with open(EVIDENCE / name, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as handle: # DictReader uses the first line (the header) to name the columns of every row. reader = csv.DictReader(handle) # Line 1 is the header, so the first data row is line 2: keep that number for the references. return [(number, row) for number, row in enumerate(reader, start=2)] # Any other row is described with its action, its target, its actor and its ticket if there is one. else: # For example "Policy applied on WS-10-22 by system" or "Policy modified on Studio-WS by contractor-it (CH-2026-089)". meaning = f"{row['action']} on {row['target']} by {row['actor']}" + (f" ({row['ticket']})" if row["ticket"] else "") # The last contact with the console: the workstation is switched on and connected. add(to_edt(row["last_seen_utc"]), "E-02", "av-console_device-status_2026-10-13.csv", number, ",".join(row.values()), f"{row['device']}: online, real-time protection {row['realtime_protection']}") # E-05: the events of the workstations; repeated identical failures are grouped to keep the timeline readable. failures = {} # The last successful update of each workstation will be kept here. last_success = {} # A later success replaces an earlier one, so only the last success remains at the end. last_success[row["Computer"]] = (number, row) # Event 2001 means "the security intelligence update failed". if row["EventId"] == "2001": # Collect the failures of each workstation in a list, in time order. failures.setdefault(row["Computer"], []).append((number, row)) # Add the last success of each workstation: the moment just before the problem started. for computer, (number, row) in last_success.items(): # Turn each list of failures into two timeline rows: the first failure and the last one, with the count. for computer, rows in failures.items(): # The first failure shows when the problem started and what the error says. first_line, first = rows[0] # The last failure shows that the problem was still present at collection time. last_line, last = rows[-1] # Add the first failure, quoted verbatim. add(to_edt(first["TimeCreated"]), "E-05", "ws-render_defender-events_2026-10-08_13.csv", first_line, ",".join(first.values()), f"{computer}: FIRST failure, source {first['UpdateSource']} {first['SourcePath']}, error {first['ErrorCode']} ({first['ErrorDescription']})") # Add the last failure with the number of identical failures in between (one every 4 hours). add(to_edt(last["TimeCreated"]), "E-05", "ws-render_defender-events_2026-10-08_13.csv", last_line, ",".join(last.values()), f"{computer}: LAST failure, {len(rows)} identical failures every 4 hours") # E-06: the transcript of SRV-AD01; its collection time is written in its first line. text = (EVIDENCE / "srv-ad01_shares_2026-10-13.txt").read_text(encoding="utf-8") # Find the date and the time in the header line, for example "2026-10-13 09:20". found = re.search(r"(\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}) (\d{2}:\d{2})", text) # Find the line that carries the error message of Get-SmbShare. error_line = [line for line in text.splitlines() if "No MSFT_SMBShare" in line][0] # Add the event: the share that the policy points to does not exist. add(to_edt(found.group(1) + " " + found.group(2)), "E-06", "srv-ad01_shares_2026-10-13.txt", text.splitlines().index(error_line) + 1, error_line, "The share \\\\SRV-AD01\\AVDefs does not exist (Test-Path D:\\AVDefs = False)") # Print the timeline, one numbered line per event. for index, event in enumerate(events, start=1): # Number, local time, evidence identifier and interpretation. print(f" {index:>2} {show(event['time'])} {event['evidence_id']} {event['interpretation']}") # Give the sorted timeline to the next steps. return events # STEP 3 - BENIGN EXPLANATIONS FIRST: each hypothesis makes a prediction; the evidence confirms or refutes it.def step3_hypotheses(): # Print the title of the step. print("STEP 3 - TEST THE BENIGN EXPLANATIONS FIRST (then the adversary hypothesis)") # Read the device status, the update history, the audit, the events, the change log and the calendar. status = {row["device"]: row for _, row in read_rows("av-console_device-status_2026-10-13.csv")} # The daily totals of successful and failed updates per workstation. history = [row for _, row in read_rows("av-console_update-history_2026-10-08_13.csv")] # The console audit (policy changes, sign-ins, alerts). audit = [row for _, row in read_rows("av-console_audit_2026-10-01_13.csv")] # The failures (event 2001) of the three workstations. fails = [row for _, row in read_rows("ws-render_defender-events_2026-10-08_13.csv") if row["EventId"] == "2001"] # The contractor's tickets, indexed by ticket number. tickets = {row["ticket"]: row for _, row in read_rows("change-log_contractor_2026-10.csv")} # The maintenance calendar as one block of text, to search for the ticket number. calendar = (EVIDENCE / "maintenance_calendar.csv").read_text(encoding="utf-8") # The text of the SRV-AD01 transcript, to check whether the share exists. shares = (EVIDENCE / "srv-ad01_shares_2026-10-13.txt").read_text(encoding="utf-8") # Prepare the list of results. results = [] # H1 (benign): the three workstations were switched off or disconnected. seen_after = all(to_edt(status[a]["last_seen_utc"]) > datetime(2026, 10, 13, 0, 0, tzinfo=EDT) for a in ASSETS) # If they were off, they would not try to update; count the update attempts that failed. attempts = len(fails) # The prediction of H1 is contradicted by both facts. h1 = "REFUTED" if seen_after and attempts > 0 else "SUPPORTED" # Record the hypothesis, its prediction, the test, the evidence and the result. results.append({"id": "H1", "kind": "benign", "hypothesis": "The three workstations were switched off or disconnected", "prediction": "No contact with the console and no update attempt after Thursday", "evidence": f"E-02: all three online on Tuesday morning; E-05: {attempts} failed attempts, one every 4 hours", "groups": ["console", "workstations"], "result": h1}) # H2 (benign): the publisher's update service was down for everybody. others_ok = sum(int(row["successful_updates"]) for row in history if row["device"] not in ASSETS and row["date"] >= "2026-10-09") # If the service were down, the other workstations would fail too during the same days. h2 = "REFUTED" if others_ok > 0 else "SUPPORTED" # Record H2. results.append({"id": "H2", "kind": "benign", "hypothesis": "The publisher's update service was unavailable", "prediction": "Every workstation fails during the same period", "evidence": f"E-03: the nine other workstations made {others_ok} successful updates from Oct 9 to Oct 13", "groups": ["console"], "result": h2}) # H3 (benign): a documented change explains the failures. ticket = tickets["CH-2026-090"] # The change must concern exactly the three assets of the alert. same_assets = all(a in ticket["assets"] for a in ASSETS) # The console audit must show the change of the update source to the file share. changed = [row for row in audit if row["action"] == "Policy modified" and "AVDefs" in row["details"]] # The workstations must report that exact source in their error messages. error_matches = all(row["UpdateSource"] == "File share" and row["SourcePath"].endswith("AVDefs") for row in fails) # The server must confirm that the share does not exist. share_missing = "No MSFT_SMBShare objects found" in shares and "False" in shares # All four observations must agree for H3 to be supported. h3 = "SUPPORTED" if same_assets and changed and error_matches and share_missing else "NOT SUPPORTED" # Record H3 with its evidence; the calendar check explains why triage could not recognize it. results.append({"id": "H3", "kind": "benign", "hypothesis": "A documented change (CH-2026-090) explains the failures", "prediction": "A change on these 3 assets before the first failure, and errors that point to the changed setting", "evidence": f"E-07: CH-2026-090 lists the 3 assets, only step 2 done, no verification; E-04: policy changed to \\\\SRV-AD01\\AVDefs at 17:42 EDT; E-05: every failure names that path, error 0x80070035; E-06: the share does not exist; E-08: CH-2026-090 in calendar = {'CH-2026-090' in calendar}", "groups": ["change-log", "console", "workstations", "srv-ad01"], "result": h3}) # H4 (adversary): someone tampered with the antivirus (MITRE ATT&CK T1685 Disable or Modify Tools). actor_known = all(row["actor"] == "contractor-it" and row["source_ip"] == "203.0.113.150" for row in changed) # The implementer written in the ticket must be the same account and address. ticket_matches = "contractor-it" in ticket["implementer"] and "203.0.113.150" in ticket["implementer"] # An adversary usually turns protection off; check that real-time protection stayed on. protection_on = all(status[a]["realtime_protection"] == "On" for a in ASSETS) # Records cannot prove who typed: a stolen console account would leave the same record. h4 = "NOT SUPPORTED (confirm by phone)" if actor_known and ticket_matches and protection_on else "OPEN" # Record H4; the remaining doubt becomes an open question for the conclusion. results.append({"id": "H4", "kind": "adversary", "hypothesis": "Someone tampered with the antivirus (ATT&CK T1685 Disable or Modify Tools, tactic TA0112 Defense Impairment)", "prediction": "Unknown account or address, protection turned off, or no matching ticket", "evidence": "E-04: change by contractor-it from 203.0.113.150 (same address as CH-2026-089); E-07: same implementer; E-02: real-time protection On on the three workstations", "groups": ["console", "change-log"], "result": h4}) # Print each hypothesis with its result. for item in results: # One line per hypothesis: identifier, result, statement. print(f" {item['id']} [{item['kind']:<9}] {item['result']:<32} {item['hypothesis']}") # Give the results to steps 4 and 5. return results # STEP 4 - CORROBORATE: the supported explanation must rest on at least two independent systems.def step4_corroborate(results): # Print the title of the step. print("STEP 4 - CORROBORATE with independent sources (two records of the same system count once)") # Find the hypothesis that the evidence supports. supported = [item for item in results if item["result"] == "SUPPORTED"] # If nothing is supported, the analysis is not finished: more evidence must be collected. if not supported: # Say so clearly and stop the corroboration here. print(" no hypothesis supported -> collect more evidence") # Return an empty result. return None, 0 # Take the supported hypothesis (only one in this case). best = supported[0] # Count the independent groups that support it. groups = sorted(set(best["groups"])) # Show which independent systems record the same facts. print(f" {best['id']} is supported by {len(groups)} independent groups: {', '.join(groups)} (minimum required: 2)") # Give the hypothesis and the number of groups to step 5. return best, len(groups) # STEP 5 - CONCLUDE: category, ATT&CK technique if there is an attacker, confidence, open questions.def step5_conclude(timeline, results, best, groups): # Print the title of the step. print("STEP 5 - CONCLUDE (preliminary; the diagnosis record of lesson 5.4 makes it final)") # Confidence grows with the number of independent groups that agree (and no contradiction). confidence = "high" if groups >= 3 else ("medium" if groups == 2 else "low") # The adversary hypothesis is not supported, so no technique is assigned. technique = None # The first failure and the last failure define the exposure window known so far. failures = [event for event in timeline if "failure" in event["interpretation"]] # The earliest failure of the three workstations. start = min(event["time"] for event in failures) # The latest failure seen in the evidence. end = max(event["time"] for event in failures) # Start an empty dictionary: it will hold everything lesson 5.4 needs to write the diagnosis record. findings = {} # The alert that was analyzed. findings["case"] = "A-09" # The preliminary category: a protection tool fails, and no unauthorized actor is supported. findings["category"] = "monitoring failure" # One sentence that says what happened, in facts. findings["summary"] = "Not an attack: the antivirus of WS-10-22, WS-10-37 and WS-10-51 could not update because policy Render-WS points to a share that was never created (change CH-2026-090, step 1 not done)." # The hypothesis that the evidence supports (H3). findings["supported_hypothesis"] = best["id"] if best else None # The number of independent groups that support it. findings["independent_groups"] = groups # The confidence level computed above. findings["confidence"] = confidence # No ATT&CK technique is assigned, because no adversary activity is supported. findings["attack_technique"] = technique # The technique that was tested anyway, with its result, so that the reader sees it was considered. findings["techniques_tested"] = [{"id": "T1685", "name": "Disable or Modify Tools", "tactic": "Defense Impairment (TA0112)", "result": results[3]["result"]}] # The start of the exposure window: the first failed update. findings["exposure_start"] = start.isoformat() # The last failure seen in the evidence collected on Tuesday morning. findings["last_failure_seen"] = end.isoformat() # The priority after analysis: the gap is confirmed (confidence 5) on assets of impact 2. findings["priority_after_analysis"] = "P2 (impact 2 x confidence 5 = 10)" # The questions that remain open; every honest conclusion lists them. findings["open_questions"] = ["Confirm by phone, at the number in the service contract, that contractor-it made the change of Thursday 17:42", "Run a full scan on the three workstations once the definitions are updated", "Why was step 1 never done, and why was CH-2026-090 not entered in the maintenance calendar?"] # Print the conclusion in four lines. print(f" category: {findings['category']} | ATT&CK: none (T1685 tested: {results[3]['result']}) | confidence: {confidence}") # Print the exposure window known at collection time. print(f" exposure so far: {show(start)} -> {show(end)} ({(end - start).days} days {(end - start).seconds // 3600} h)") # Print the priority recommendation: the gap is now confirmed, so A-09 moves from P3 to P2. print(f" priority: triage P3 -> {findings['priority_after_analysis']}") # Print the open questions, which are part of every conclusion. for question in findings["open_questions"]: # One open question per line. print(" open:", question) # Give the findings to the function that saves the files. return findings # Define the function that saves the three output files.def save(timeline, results, findings): # Create the output folder if it does not exist yet. OUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True) # Open the timeline file for writing; "newline=''" avoids blank lines on Windows. with open(OUT / "a09_timeline.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as handle: # A csv writer quotes the fields that contain commas. writer = csv.writer(handle) # Header: the four columns required by Lab 3 Part C, plus references and UTC time. writer.writerow(["n", "time_edt", "time_utc", "evidence_id", "file", "line", "record_verbatim", "interpretation"]) # One row per event, in time order. for index, event in enumerate(timeline, start=1): # Write the local time, the UTC time, the reference, the verbatim record and its meaning. writer.writerow([index, show(event["time"]), event["time"].astimezone(timezone.utc).strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"), event["evidence_id"], event["file"], event["line"], event["record"], event["interpretation"]]) # Open the hypothesis file for writing. with open(OUT / "a09_hypotheses.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as handle: # A csv writer for the hypothesis table. writer = csv.writer(handle) # Header of the hypothesis table. writer.writerow(["id", "kind", "hypothesis", "prediction", "evidence", "independent_groups", "result"]) # One row per hypothesis. for item in results: # Write the row. writer.writerow([item["id"], item["kind"], item["hypothesis"], item["prediction"], item["evidence"], "; ".join(item["groups"]), item["result"]]) # Save the findings as JSON, readable by the PowerShell script of lesson 5.4. (OUT / "a09_findings.json").write_text(json.dumps(findings, indent=2), encoding="utf-8") # Confirm where the files are. print(f"saved: {OUT / 'a09_timeline.csv'}, a09_hypotheses.csv, a09_findings.json") # The main block runs the five steps in order, exactly as the lesson presents them.if __name__ == "__main__": # Step 1: collect. evidence = step1_collect() # Step 2: timeline. events = step2_timeline() # Step 3: benign explanations first. tested = step3_hypotheses() # Step 4: corroborate the supported explanation. explanation, independent = step4_corroborate(tested) # Step 5: conclude. result = step5_conclude(events, tested, explanation, independent) # Save the three outputs. save(events, tested, result)

Step-by-step explanation of analyze_anomaly.py

  1. Preparation. The script imports five standard modules (csv, json, re, datetime, pathlib), locates the folders a09_evidence and outputs next to its own folder, and defines the EDT (Eastern Daylight Time) offset (UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) − 4 hours) and the three assets.
  2. Helpers. to_edt() reads any time of the pack (UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) with Z, local with an offset, or local without offset) and returns it in EDT (Eastern Daylight Time); show() formats it the same way everywhere; read_rows() reads a CSV (comma-separated values) file and adds the line number of each record, so that every row of the timeline can point to its source line.
  3. Step 1, collect. step1_collect() reads collection_log.csv, keeps the files whose phase is analysis, checks that each file is present and prints its independence group. Result: 8 files from 5 groups.
  4. Step 2, timeline. step2_timeline() takes the useful records of each file, converts their times to EDT (Eastern Daylight Time), keeps the text of each record verbatim and writes one interpretation. For the 84 failures it keeps only the first and the last per workstation, with the count. It sorts the 30 rows by time.
  5. Step 3, hypotheses. step3_hypotheses() tests H1, H2 and H3 (benign) and then H4 (adversary). Each test is a small computation on the evidence: is the workstation online, did the other workstations update, did a change touch these assets before the first failure, which account and address made it.
  6. Step 4, corroborate. step4_corroborate() counts the distinct independence groups behind the supported hypothesis (4) and compares the count with the minimum (2).
  7. Step 5, conclude. step5_conclude() writes the category, the confidence, the exposure measured from the first and the last failure, the priority (impact 2 × confidence 5 = 10, P2 (priority 2)) and the open questions.
  8. Save. save() writes the three output files in outputs/; the evidence folder is never modified.

5.4

Diagnosing incidents and documenting the findings

Slide 23

The analysis produced findings. The diagnosis turns them into a decision that other people can act on: what kind of problem this is, why it happened, how far it reached, what it cost or could have cost, and how urgent it is. The documentation makes that decision checkable, today and months later.

Slide 24

5.4.1 Key terms

Event
Any observable occurrence in a system or a network: a logon, an update, a change of policy.
Security incident
NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-61 Revision 3 uses the definition of the United States Federal Information Security Modernization Act of 2014: "an occurrence that actually or imminently jeopardizes, without lawful authority, the integrity, confidentiality, or availability of information or an information system; or constitutes a violation or imminent threat of violation of law, security policies, security procedures, or acceptable use policies." The NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) glossary also lists older variants of this text; this module uses the one above everywhere.
Monitoring failure
A monitoring or protection tool stops collecting data or stops protecting, without an attacker: logs not collected, agent stopped, disk full, updates failing. It is not an attack, but it opens a period during which an attack would be neither detected nor blocked.
Benign true positive
The rule worked correctly, on activity that is authorized and expected (Class 15). A false positive is different: the rule itself is wrong.
Diagnosis
The documented decision about what an anomaly is: category, root cause, scope, impact, priority, adversary technique if there is an attacker, and confidence.
Diagnosis record
The document that contains the diagnosis and the references of the evidence behind each statement.
Slide 25

5.4.2 Three questions decide the category

  1. Question 1. Did someone act without authority, or was a security policy violated? Yes: security incident.
  2. Question 2. Is a monitoring or protection tool failing? Yes: monitoring failure.
  3. Question 3. Was the activity authorized and expected? Yes: benign.

The questions are asked in this order and the first "yes" decides. A monitoring failure caused by an attacker, for example an intruder who stops the antivirus, is a security incident, because Question 1 comes first. If the answer is "no" to all three questions, the analysis is not finished: collect more evidence and repeat the steps of lesson 5.3.

A-09: Question 1 is "no": the change was made by the contractor's account, from its usual address, under the approved ticket CH-2026-090, and the contractor confirmed it by phone at 09:50, at the number written in the service contract. Question 2 is "yes": three workstations had definitions 4.5 days old. Category: monitoring failure.

Table 5.4-1 - The three diagnosis categories
CategoryDefinitionTypical evidenceExamples in this courseWhat followsLegal notification check
Security incidentAn occurrence that actually or imminently jeopardizes, without lawful authority, the confidentiality, integrity or availability of information or of a system, or that violates a law, a security policy or an acceptable use policy (the definition used by NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-61 Revision 3, summarized).An account used by someone who is not its owner; a malicious program; data accessed, changed or sent without authorityPassword guessing that succeeds; a malicious program started by a userContain, eradicate, recover; map ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge) techniques; preserve evidenceAlways check (Law 25 if personal information is involved)
Monitoring failureA monitoring or protection tool stops collecting data or stops protecting, without an attacker.Missing logs, stopped agent, full disk, failed updates, broken ruleA-09: antivirus definitions not updated for 4.5 daysFix the tool, verify the fix with evidence, write the lessons learnedUsually nothing to notify; record the reasoning
BenignAuthorized and expected activity: the rule fired correctly (benign true positive), or the rule itself was wrong (false positive).A calendar entry, a ticket, an allow-list line, a logbook entryA-04 nightly backup, A-10 typing errors then success, A-11 vendor mirror download (Class 15)Close with the reason; tune the rule or add a scoped exception (Topic 6.4)Nothing to notify
The three categories are the ones Lab 3, Part C asks for. The decision questions are asked in this order: unauthorized actor? tool failing? authorized activity?
Slide 26

5.4.3 Root cause

  • The immediate cause is the condition that directly produced the symptom. A-09: the update source of the policy points to a share that does not exist.
  • The root cause is the most basic cause that, once removed, would have prevented the problem and will prevent it from coming back. Find it by asking "why?" until the answer is a decision or a process that people can change:
  1. Why did the updates fail? The workstations searched for definitions in \\SRV-AD01\AVDefs, which does not exist (E-05, E-06).
  2. Why does the policy point there? Step 2 of change CH-2026-090 was applied on Thursday at 17:42 (E-04, E-07).
  3. Why does the share not exist? Step 1, create the share and its copy job, planned for Friday at 09:00, was never done (E-07).
  4. Why did nobody notice before Saturday? The ticket had no verification step, and the change was not in the maintenance calendar. The device-health check runs once a day, at 09:30, and reports a workstation only after more than 24 hours without a successful update. On Friday at 09:30 the last success (Thursday 17:15) was 16 hours old, so the first alert came on Saturday at 09:30.

Root cause of A-09: the change process allowed a change to be applied without a verification step and without an entry in the maintenance calendar. Contributing factors: step 2 was done before step 1, and the policy kept no second update source (the Microsoft documentation on update sources describes the fallback order that was removed). A root cause is written as a fact about a process, not as a judgment about a person: "step 1 was skipped and nothing checked it" leads to a better process; "the contractor is careless" names nothing that a process change can fix.

Slide 27

5.4.4 Scope and exposure window

  • The scope is the set of assets, accounts and data affected. A-09: three workstations; no account; no data accessed, changed or lost.
  • The exposure window is the period during which the weakness existed, measured from evidence: from the first moment of exposure to the verified end. A-09: from the first failed update (Thursday 21:15, when the workstations should have received new definitions and did not) to the last workstation updated after the fix (Tuesday 10:46): 4 days 13 hours 31 minutes.
  • The detection delay is the time between the start of the exposure and the alert: Thursday 21:15 to Saturday 09:30, that is 36 hours 15 minutes.
  • Why measure from evidence? The alert time (Saturday 09:30) would leave out 36 hours of exposure. The time of the change (17:42) would add 3.5 hours during which the definitions were still current, because they had been updated at 17:15.
Slide 28

5.4.5 Impact and priority after diagnosis

Rate the impact on each of the three properties of information security, known together as CIA (confidentiality, integrity, availability). Use three levels: none, potential (possible, but not observed) and confirmed (observed in the evidence).

Table 5.4-2 - Impact on confidentiality, integrity and availability (CIA)
PropertyQuestion to askNonePotentialConfirmedA-09
ConfidentialityCould someone see information they are not allowed to see?No access possible or observedAccess was possible, not observedAccess observed in the evidenceNone observed
IntegrityCould information or a system be changed without authority?No change possible or observedA change was possible, not observedA change observedPotential: a new threat would not have been recognized
AvailabilityCould people lose access to information or systems?No interruptionAn interruption was possibleAn interruption observedNone observed
The rating feeds the impact value (1 to 5) of the priority calculation: see the sheet PRIORITY_CALC of the XLSX (Excel workbook file) file.

A-09: confidentiality, none observed; integrity, potential, because a new threat would not have been recognized for 4.5 days; availability, none observed.

The priority after diagnosis uses the same scale as the triage of lesson 5.2: impact × confidence, with four bands: 16 or more is P1 (priority 1), 10 to 15 is P2 (priority 2), 5 to 9 is P3 (priority 3), and 4 or less is P4 (priority 4). At triage, A-09 had 2 × 3 = 6, band P3 (priority 3). After diagnosis the impact stays 2 (workstations, criticality 2), but the confidence that the problem is real rises to 5, because four independent groups prove it: 2 × 5 = 10, band P2 (priority 2) ("today"). The hand rule of lesson 5.2 (a manual rule that the analyst applies after the score) says that an alert about the health of monitoring or protection is never below P2 (priority 2): applied at triage, it would already have placed A-09 in P2 (priority 2), while the score alone (6) put it in P3 (priority 3). The fix was made the same morning.

Slide 29

5.4.6 Adversary behaviour and confidence

  • Assign a MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge) technique only when evidence shows the behaviour. Also write the techniques you tested and refuted: they show what was checked.
  • Version matters. In ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge) version 19, current since April 28, 2026 (version history), the tactic TA0005 is named Stealth, and a new tactic, TA0112 Defense Impairment, groups the techniques that degrade or disable security controls and monitoring. Its technique T1685 Disable or Modify Tools includes stopping security services, changing their configuration and blocking their updates. Older documents (ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge) version 18 and earlier) cite T1562.001, Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools, under the former tactic Defense Evasion, for the same behaviour; version 19 merged it into T1685. Always write the version you used.
  • A-09: no technique assigned; T1685 tested and refuted (change confirmed out of band, approved ticket, usual account and address).

Table 5.4-4 - Confidence levels
LevelCriteriaWording to useExample
HighThree or more independent groups agree; no record contradicts; the mechanism is explained"The evidence shows that..."A-09: workstations, console, SRV-AD01 and change log agree
MediumTwo independent groups agree, or one gap remains"The evidence indicates that..." / "probably"A host log and a firewall log agree, but the process is unknown
LowOne source only, or sources disagree"One record suggests that..." / "possibly"A single alert with no corroboration yet
A confidence level is a statement about the evidence, not about the analyst: it changes when new evidence arrives.
Slide 30

5.4.7 Documenting: the diagnosis record

One record per case, written while you work, not from memory afterwards. It has eleven sections:

Table 5.4-5 - Sections of a diagnosis record
SectionWhat it containsA-09 (CASE-2026-016)Lab 3: C_diagnosis.md
1 What happenedFacts only, in two to four sentencesDefinitions not updated on three workstations; not an attackRequired
2 CategoryThe category and the answer to each decision question, with evidence identifiersMonitoring failure (Question 1 no, Question 2 yes)Required
3 Root causeThe cause that, once removed, prevents the problem from coming backCH-2026-090: step 2 done without step 1; no verification; not in the calendarRequired
4 Scope and exposure windowAssets, accounts, data; start and end of the exposure, measured from evidence3 workstations; Thu 21:15 to Tue 10:46 (4 d 13 h 31 min)Required
5 Impact and priorityConfidentiality, integrity, availability; priority before and after diagnosisC none, I potential, A none; P3 (priority 3) to P2 (priority 2)Required
6 Adversary behaviourMITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge) technique(s) supported by evidence, or the techniques tested and refutedNone; T1685 tested and refutedRequired if there is an attacker
7 ConfidenceLow, medium or high, with the reasonHigh: 4 independent groups, no contradictionRequired
8 Key timelineThe key records with file and line; the full timeline attached13 key rows; a09_timeline.csvRequired (timeline table)
9 Actions takenContemporaneous log: time, who, action, result10 actions from 08:55 to 13:00Recommended
10 Evidence registerIdentifier, file, source, collector, time, SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit)E-01 to E-11Recommended
11 Open questions and lessonsWhat stays open; what to change (Topic 6)4 lessons for the review of FridayRequired (open questions)
The template templates/C_diagnosis_template.md has the same eleven sections.
  • Facts and interpretations are written separately. A fact is what the evidence shows, with its reference; an interpretation is what you conclude from it.
  • Every fact has a reference: evidence identifier, file and line.
  • The actions log is contemporaneous: each action is written at the time it is done, with the time, the person, the action and the result.
  • Uncertainty is stated with the confidence level and the open questions.
  • The record is labelled and protected. The A-09 record carries TLP:AMBER+STRICT (Traffic Light Protocol) and is stored with need-to-know access, because monitoring data are treated as personal information (Legal Notice, section 7.2).
Slide 31

5.4.8 Evidence integrity and chain of custody

  • A hash value is a fixed-length number computed from the bytes of a file. With SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit) (NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standard) 180-4) the value has 256 bits, written as 64 hexadecimal characters. The same bytes always give the same value; changing a single byte changes the value almost completely; and it is computationally infeasible to build a different file with the same value.
  • The evidence register lists every evidence file with its hash, size, source, collector, time and method.
  • Integrity verification means computing the hash again later and comparing it with the register. Equal values show that the file is byte-for-byte the one that was collected.
  • The chain of custody is the record of every person who held the evidence, when and why, from collection to the end of the case (RFC (Request for Comments) 3227; NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-86).
  • Practice: keep the originals read-only, work on copies, and never open an evidence file with a program that saves automatically. A spreadsheet program that reformats dates and saves the file changes its bytes and its hash.
  • Demonstration: on a copy of E-08, the word "Nightly" was changed to "Mightly". One letter changed; 60 of the 64 characters of the hash changed.
